extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists and students interested in media controversies and editorial cartoons
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia encyclopedia article cataloguing notable incidents and types of controversial newspaper caricatures across countries, describing examples, reactions, and legal/social consequences. The page summarizes why certain cartoons provoked controversy and records outcomes (protests, legal action, apologies, bans).

rubrics_metrics.name: Depicting the Islamic prophet Muhammad
rubrics_metrics.description: The Jyllands-Posten Muhammad cartoons controversy — unflattering depictions of the Islamic prophet Muhammad first published in Denmark in September 2005 ... led to wide-scale protesting and rioting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing images of Muhammad has a high risk of provoking large-scale protests and violent reactions in some communities; subsequent publications and responses may escalate (e.g., other outlets publishing provocative replies, or international diplomatic fallout).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Holocaust denial or Holocaust analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include publication of cartoons suggesting Holocaust denial in response to the Muhammad cartoons, and a Le Monde cartoon comparing destruction after the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising with destruction in Jenin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies to the Holocaust or imagery that suggests denial are highly sensitive and frequently criticized; they can trigger accusations of antisemitism and widespread condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antisemitic themes and Nazi-style propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Many newspapers (noted especially in the Middle East section) have frequently published cartoons with allegedly antisemitic themes, or those created or inspired by Nazi-style propaganda, often portraying Israeli Jews or Israeli leaders as Nazis or using dehumanizing metaphors (spiders, octopuses, scorpions, snakes, thieves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depicting a group with Nazi comparisons or recurring dehumanizing tropes tends to be classified as antisemitic/racist and is a common ground for complaint and controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depicting politicians in sexual acts or humiliating contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: El Jueves published a front-page cartoon of Crown Prince Felipe having sex with his wife; Judge Juan del Olmo ruled that the cartoon 'struck at the honour and dignity of the people represented.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sexualized or humiliating portrayals of public figures can provoke legal complaints on grounds of honour/dignity and may result in court rulings, censorship requests, or bans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depicting religious figures in sexual or degrading contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: The student newspaper The Sheaf published a cartoon showing Jesus performing a sexual act with a pig; the paper apologized and the editor resigned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portraying sacred religious figures in sexual or degrading ways commonly triggers public outrage, demands for apologies, resignations, or other institutional consequences, even when intended as political satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Racist caricatures using exaggerated features
rubrics_metrics.description: Racist caricatures of African Americans in the U.S. and exaggerated depictions of Japanese people during World War II (and other ethnic caricatures) have appeared and remained controversial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using stereotyped, exaggerated physical traits or dehumanizing imagery of ethnic/racial groups is historically associated with racism and can lead to long-term reputational harm and public backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diplomatic or reciprocal provocations via national/leader depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: Indonesian and Australian newspapers exchanged cartoons depicting each other's leaders or populations as animals (dingoes, dogs copulating with Papuans), provoking mutual response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derogatory portrayals of foreign leaders or peoples can escalate into diplomatic incidents or reciprocal satirical attacks; cross-border sensitivity varies by country and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial watchdog and press-complaint evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Press Watchdog / press complaints commission evaluated whether certain cartoons were inherently antisemitic (example: The Independent cartoon of Ariel Sharon was contested and reviewed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent press regulators and watchdogs assess cartoons for standards like hate speech, discrimination, and context/intent; their findings influence whether a cartoon is censured or defended as legitimate satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government censorship, suspension, or legal action
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments have suspended or banned publications over cartoons (example: Iranian government suspended a state-owned newspaper after a 'cockroach' cartoon; judges have ruled against cartoons on honour/dignity grounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State actors may impose censorship, bans, or prosecutions in response to cartoons deemed offensive or threatening public order; legal regimes and thresholds differ widely between countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of speech / national norms affecting acceptability
rubrics_metrics.description: In some countries (example: Mexican cartoonists) broad freedom of speech allows publication of content that may be normal locally but controversial elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local legal protections for press freedom and cultural norms shape what is publishable; what is tolerated in one country may provoke legal or social sanction in another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and institutional responses to controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical outcomes recorded include public protests and rioting, formal complaints by embassies or governments, apologies by editors, resignations, bans/suspensions, and selection for awards (e.g., Cartoon of the Year despite controversy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or producing controversial cartoons, anticipate a range of responses—from institutional defense and awards to legal action and violent protest—depending on context, subject, and audience sensitivity.
